newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia signals tougher defence strategy.
newsitem.headline: Australia signals tougher defence strategy.

text.p: Australia, shifting towards a more hawkish defence strategy, said on Sunday its forces could fight anywhere to defend Australian freedoms, including regional flare-ups and helping allies with internal conflicts.

Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said Canberra must be ready to combat a threat anywhere in the world, a marked shift from the former Labor administration's focus on defending this vast nation's coastline and sea approaches.

McLachlan said in a television interview he could not rule out military involvement anywhere, including potential conflicts on the Korean peninsula or between China and Taiwan, or internal disputes in allied countries.
But he cautioned there was currently no specific threat and Australia's strategic planning looked 10 to 15 years ahead.

"All we're saying is that we need to make sure that we have mobility, both on this continent and off it, and that...if freedom, if you like, liberty or the way that we've liked to live our lives over the last 40 or 50 years is threatened anywhere in the world, we have to consider that," he said.
Australia had to prepare for a range of potential security threats, McLachlan said.

"It may be a country, it may be piracy, it may be some firefight, as I call them, that breaks out, that nobody's thought of yet," he said. "It may be an internal problem that a country has who is a friend of ours.
"It is not impossible that, years from now, that some internal problem occurs somewhere where some of our friends ask for our help," he said.

The year-old conservative Liberal-National government is more hawkish on defence than Labor, boosting combat ability, shielding the A$10 billion (US$7.75 billion) annual budget from cutbacks, shifting more spending to weapons and strengthening security pacts with its allies, including the United States.
Australia and Japan will also discuss increased military co-operation during a visit by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, due to arrive on Monday, McLachlan said.
McLachlan's comments came a day after a newspaper reported a secret defence review had urged a more assertive regional role and stronger air power and offshore combat capability.
McLachlan said the government's response to the review would be unveiled late this year.

The government, strapped for cash while watching regional neighbours spend big on defence, two weeks ago announced its biggest military shake-up in 25 years, slashing the bureaucracy and boosting combat strength.
Australia remains one of the most powerful military forces in a region rife with internal tensions fuelled by ethnic, political and religious divisions.

Indonesia, just a few hundred kilometres to the north and long regarded as the most strategically important country to Australia, faces three low-level secessionist revolts -- in Aceh in the west and East Timor and Irian Jaya in the east.
Australia's nearest neighbour, Papua New Guinea, was last month rocked by an army mutiny that forced Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan and key government figures to step aside.
